title: Mumbai

places.name: Mumbai
places.summary: India's city of dreams: three World Heritage Sites, the Gateway of India and Marine Drive, Elephanta by ferry, and some of the country's best street food.
places.seoTitle: Mumbai Travel Guide: Gateway of India, Elephanta & Food
places.seoDescription: Plan your Mumbai trip: the Gateway of India, Elephanta Caves, CSMT and the Art Deco Fort area, Marine Drive, when to go, local trains and metro, food and safety.

images.alt: The lights of Marine Drive curving along the bay at dusk, with Mumbai's skyline behind
images.caption: Marine Drive, the 'Queen's Necklace'

overview.text:
Mumbai began as seven islands on the Arabian Sea, passed from the Portuguese to the British Crown as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry, and grew into India's commercial capital. It is a city of contrasts: Gothic railway stations and Art Deco apartment blocks, skyscrapers and street-food stalls, Bollywood studios and centuries-old shrines.

Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites are within easy reach — the rock-cut Elephanta Caves, an hour's ferry ride across the harbour, and in the old Fort district, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco ensembles around the Oval Maidan. Add the Gateway of India, an evening on Marine Drive and a plate of vada pav, and you have the classic first visit.

October to February is the most comfortable time to come. The monsoon, from June to September, brings heavy rain and sometimes flooding, but also the build-up to Ganesh Chaturthi, the city's biggest festival.

items.body: The Gateway of India on the harbour, and the ferry from there to the Elephanta Caves.
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, a working Gothic Revival railway station.
The Victorian Gothic and Art Deco buildings around the Oval Maidan.
Sunset on Marine Drive, the 'Queen's Necklace'.
Street food at Chowpatty and Mohammed Ali Road.

best_time.text: The Ministry of Tourism recommends October to February, when temperatures are mild and evenings breezy. The south-west monsoon lasts from June to the end of September; it is dramatic but very wet, the city is prone to flooding, and the Elephanta ferry can be rough. Festivals are a draw in their own right: Ganesh Chaturthi, a 10-day celebration after the monsoon, and the Kala Ghoda Arts Festival every February.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport is India's second-busiest, with flights across India and the world. A second airport, Navi Mumbai International, opened to commercial flights in December 2025 — check which one your flight uses.

By train: long-distance trains arrive at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Mumbai's other terminals; book on IRCTC.

local_transport.text: The suburban 'local' trains are the city's lifeline, carrying more than 7.5 million people a day; they are fast and cheap, but avoid rush hour with luggage. Women-only coaches are available. The fully underground Metro Line 3 (Aqua Line) runs from Cuffe Parade in the south to Aarey JVLR, with a stop at the international airport. Taxis, app cabs and auto-rickshaws cover the rest — agree the fare or use the meter.

where_to_stay.text: Colaba and the Fort area in South Mumbai put you within walking distance of the Gateway of India, the Art Deco district and CSMT — the best base for a short, heritage-focused stay. Bandra and Juhu, further north, are lively for food, shopping and nightlife. Getting between south and north Mumbai takes time, so choose the area that matches what you'll do most.

items.body: Vada pav — Mumbai's signature snack — plus pav bhaji, bhel puri and sev puri.
Misal pav for a spicy breakfast.
Street food at Chowpatty, Crawford Market and Mohammed Ali Road.
Take the ferry from the Gateway of India to the Elephanta Caves (closed Mondays).
Walk the Fort district: CSMT, the Rajabai Clock Tower and the Art Deco buildings around the Oval Maidan.
See the galleries of Kala Ghoda, including the Jehangir Art Gallery.
Shop at Colaba Causeway, Crawford Market and Chor Bazaar.
Escape to the forests of Sanjay Gandhi National Park.
At Siddhivinayak, Haji Ali and other places of worship, dress modestly and remove your shoes.
On local trains, let passengers off before boarding and keep bags in front of you.
Ask before photographing people, especially at places of worship.

overview.text:
The Gateway of India stands on the harbour front at Apollo Bunder, in Colaba. It was built to commemorate the landing of King George V and Queen Mary in December 1911, and was completed in 1924. Today it is Mumbai's most recognisable landmark and a favourite meeting place, busy from morning until late evening.

The Gateway is also the jetty for ferries to the Elephanta Caves, about an hour away across the harbour. The Taj Mahal Palace hotel faces it, and Nariman Point and Marine Drive are a short drive north-west. Come early in the morning for quieter photographs, or in the evening when the arch is lit.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: An open public space, accessible at any time.

items.title: Elephanta ferries
items.body: Leave from the jetties beside the Gateway; the crossing takes about an hour. The caves are closed on Mondays.

places.seoDescription: Visit the Elephanta Caves near Mumbai: the ferry from the Gateway of India, opening hours and Monday closure, the Trimurti sculpture and monsoon tips.

overview.text:
The Elephanta Caves are rock-cut temples to Shiva on Elephanta Island, about 11 km across Mumbai Harbour from the Gateway of India. They are generally dated to between the 5th and 7th centuries, though who built them is still uncertain, and they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

The main cave is the reason to come. Its walls carry monumental reliefs of Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of dance, as Ardhanarishvara, half man and half woman, and — most famously — as the three-headed Sadashiva, or Trimurti, which towers over the hall. The ferry from the Gateway takes about an hour.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9 am – 5:30 pm. Closed on Mondays.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: Ferry from the Gateway of India, about one hour each way.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: There is an entry fee; check the current amount on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site.

items.title: Monsoon
items.body: Crossings can be rough and paths slippery from June to September.
Take an early ferry to beat the crowds and the midday heat.
Allow about half a day in total, including the ferry.
Wear shoes with good grip — paths can be wet and slippery in the monsoon.

places.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus
places.summary: Mumbai's Gothic Revival railway terminus of 1887, still one of India's busiest stations — and a World Heritage Site.
places.seoDescription: See Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Mumbai's UNESCO-listed Gothic Revival railway station: its history, F. W. Stevens's design and what to look for.

images.alt: The long Gothic Revival front of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus with its central dome
images.caption: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus

overview.text:
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, formerly Victoria Terminus, was built in 1887 for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee and is one of Mumbai's three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The architect, Frederick William Stevens, blended Victorian Italianate Gothic Revival with traditional Indian architecture: towers and spires recall European cathedrals, while the C-shaped plan is borrowed from Indian palaces.

It is still very much a working station — the headquarters of the Central Railway, used by more than 3 million people a day according to the Ministry of Tourism. Look for the lion and tiger statues at the entrance and the central dome topped by a torch-bearing figure. The best view is from across the road outside.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: A working station, open all day.

items.title: Best view
items.body: From across the road in front of the main facade.

places.name: Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles
places.summary: Two architectural eras face each other across the Oval Maidan: Victorian Gothic on one side, Art Deco on the other — a World Heritage Site since 2018.
places.seoTitle: Mumbai's Victorian Gothic & Art Deco Ensemble (UNESCO)
places.seoDescription: Walk Mumbai's UNESCO-listed Victorian Gothic and Art Deco ensembles around the Oval Maidan: the High Court, Rajabai Clock Tower, Eros Cinema and Marine Drive.

images.commons: File:Bombay High Court and Rajabai Clock Tower from Oval Maidan, Mumbai.jpg
images.alt: The Gothic Bombay High Court and Rajabai Clock Tower seen across the green Oval Maidan
images.caption: High Court and Rajabai Clock Tower from the Oval Maidan

overview.text:
Around the Oval Maidan in Mumbai's Fort district, two architectural eras face each other. On the east side stand 19th-century Victorian Gothic buildings — the Bombay High Court, the University of Mumbai's Fort campus and the Rajabai Clock Tower. On the west side are 20th-century Art Deco buildings, among them the Eros Cinema. Together they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.

The Art Deco continues along Marine Drive, lined with apartment blocks from the 1920s and 1930s. The ensemble is best seen on foot: walk across the Oval Maidan in the late afternoon, then head west to the sea for sunset.

items.body: Combine with CSMT and the Kala Ghoda galleries on a half-day walk.
Late afternoon light is best for the Gothic facades.

overview.text: Marine Drive is a 3.6 km C-shaped promenade along the sea in South Mumbai, nicknamed the Queen's Necklace for the curve of its streetlights at night. Lined with Art Deco buildings from the 1920s and 1930s, it is Mumbai's favourite place for a sunset walk. Chowpatty beach, at its northern end, is famous for street food.

overview.text: Siddhivinayak, in Prabhadevi, is one of Mumbai's most revered temples to Ganesha. It dates from the 18th century, and its idol is carved from a single black stone. It is open from 5:30 am to 10 pm; Tuesday is the busiest day, when it opens from 3:15 am. Expect queues and security checks.
